utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The events that you testified about yesterday or, rather, what Mr. Nice read out and you said was your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let us be accurate. It is her testimony because the witness gave evidence about it on a previous occasion, and that's its status, and that should be understood. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did the JNA or, rather, the members of the JNA protect the Croatian population from possible violence under the circumstances and in the situation that prevailed in Vukovar at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army went out of the barracks and advanced towards Borovo Selo. And that was in May 1991 already. It shelled Vukovar every day. It killed innocent civilians, women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are -- perhaps we could just concentrate on the question, if you would, Doctor. You're saying, then, are you, that you don't agree that they were protecting, the JNA were protecting the population. You disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I realise what Mr. Milosevic is in fact asking me and wants to ask me. He's asking me whether the Yugoslav People's Army saved any lives after the occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. Let -- please. Please just concentrate on the question. And I think you could give a fairly short answer, because what he's asking is - and this is his case - that the JNA were protecting the population at the time in Vukovar. And I think you could probably say yes or no to that, can't you? There's no need to repeat the evidence which we've already heard. That's the point I'm trying to make.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If your answer is no, then I'm asking you this: As this is your document, your statement, in fact, it's not anybody else's document, it's written in your own handwriting, and in that document, on page 2, once again written in hand by you, it says at the end: "The JNA protected the Croats from the extremists," the nationalist extremists, oriented that way, and so on and so forth. That's what you say in your own statement. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy of the statement, first of all. Have you got a copy there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I think the accused may be cross-examining from a document that the witness has not seen since its creation, but I'm not sure. Once he shows it to her she will be able to give an account of its provenance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see the document, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can have a look at part of that document because I don't have time to refer to the whole document. I'm just going to refer to certain portions of it, and you can take it as an exhibit. It is a statement written in the handwriting of the witness. In her own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since I believe I know what the document is, I'm not sure whether the accused has handed to her an incomplete version or a incomplete version. It might be important that a complete version is made available to her and to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us as to what the document is, Mr. Nice? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think we'll hear it's a document that was obtained in the course of the witness's time in custody, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear from the witness. Dr. Bosanac, can you tell us what that document is, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's the statement which I wrote when I was in detention, in custody in Serbia, in Sremska Mitrovica, in fact, and in Belgrade as well, and that's when I was duty-bound to make this kind of statement, and I wrote it down. And in that context, Mr. Milosevic asked me whether this is my opinion about some of the people who, after the occupation, were protected by the JNA. However, over 1.300 were left to the paramilitaries to kill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you write that, that over 1.300 were allowed to be killed by the paramilitaries? In that statement, you speak about --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know about that. This is something I learnt later on. I learn how many were allowed to be killed later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, are you talking about the victims that fell casualty in conflicts or some kind of execution performed over these 1.300 people?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Execution. The aggression against Vukovar was such that there were no conflicts. What did happen was the destruction of towns and civilians, and in that conflict 1.500 people. Seventy per cent of those people were civilians, and 1.300 were killed after the occupation of Vukovar when there were no more conflicts whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether the JNA perpetrated these acts, the acts that you're talking about. In your conflict, in the conflict in Vukovar, did the JNA endeavour to protect one and all equally, Serbs, Croats, Hungarians and members of other national minorities living there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why did you write that it did, then?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not write that it did protect everybody equally and partially. When the Yugoslav army occupied Vukovar, together with the paramilitary forces, it allowed the paramilitary forces to take the wounded away and kill them, and that is what Major Sljivancanin allowed, as representative of the JNA. It took over the hospital and the people were killed -- 200 people were killed at Ovcara in a very violent and brutal manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that. According to my information, the JNA has nothing to do with these killings at Ovcara, but as you know your handwriting very well, you can read for yourself what you wrote on page 2 and what I have marked with a marker pen, and the portion I quoted when I asked you my question. So you can read it out yourself what you yourself wrote in the statement.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read what it says in the statement. I haven't seen this statement since 1991. I was being interrogated while in prison, while in custody, and I cannot read out the whole statement now. If need be, I can read it out and comment every sentence of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you to read out the whole statement. I don't think there's any misunderstanding there. Just turn the first page and take a look at the bottom of the second page and you'll find the sentence that you yourself wrote in which I have marked with a marker pen.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, you have marked it as being written by me, but I say that it protected individuals, but it allowed people to be killed en masse, not only Croats but Hungarians and Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Permitted the killing of people. That's what you say?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And killed itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And killed itself. But nonetheless, read out, if you would, what you yourself wrote down. Read it out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You quoted only part of the sentence on page 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but please read it out.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what it says: "The JNA nonetheless protected the Croats from retaliation by Serb nationalists, mostly of the Chetnik orientation." That is what I wrote at the time that I was in prison, and that was in 1991. But the JNA, had it really protected the Croats, then 1.300 people would not have been killed after the occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Are you claiming that you wrote that statement under duress?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. And how come that at the end of your statement - and I'll give you this page to take a look at it for yourself - how come you say to the colonel who conducted the investigation with me and analysed the events, why do you say, "I thank him" -- then there's something that I can't read, but: "I thank him for his humane conduct and giving us hope that in the JNA there are people who wish peace and who are humane and would like to see cohabitation of all peoples living in the area. And he was highly proper in his conduct towards me as a man and towards me as a person." So this person who interrogated you did not exert any pressure. He talked to you in a proper fashion, humanely, or perhaps do you say that he forced you to write all this down?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us, first of all, deal with this in an orderly way. Before we move on from the first passage which has been read out, is there anything else from the statement? You said that it was incomplete, what you read out. Is there anything you would like to read out before we go on to deal with the next passage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I don't have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't interrupt, Mr. Milosevic. The witness should have the opportunity to deal with the matter fully.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Judge, Your Honour, this statement was written in 1991, in November and December. I was taken into custody without any reason and was kept in detention for three weeks under pressure in Serbian prisons. I have also given testimony about that to this court. I was under enormous psychological pressure. I was held in a solitary confinement cell for two days. I was completely isolated. After that, I was given the chance of writing the statement for me to be able to come into contact at all with, or to do anything for myself, to help myself leave prison. So I was under enormous pressure, under duress, and I listened how people were being beaten every day. I heard their screams and their cries, and I wrote this statement down all the days I was there. I wanted to write the whole truth. I wanted to write down that the Yugoslav army had broken up Vukovar, had killed people up until the occupation because at that time I didn't know what happened after the occupation. The Yugoslav army helped bring about the evacuation of the hospital, but that's what I said earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Bosanac, you've given evidence about that. We ought just to deal with the statement at the moment. Now, Mr. Milosevic, is there another part of the statement which you have just read out or have you got a copy of it? If not, the witness should have that section which you've read out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've got that section and what I quoted a moment ago. She can take a look at it, because she's talking about some terrible treatment there. However, at the end, she expresses her gratitude for the humane conduct of this person and giving her hope that peace could be reached. But here you have it. Please take it and read it, read what you say at the end of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the witness is doing that and to save time, can I insist, please, on behalf of the Prosecution, that the full statement is produced. We'll then copy it. The question will arise whether it should become an exhibit or maybe that question can be determined. We must have a full copy of the whole statement, not selected bits. The Chamber will find that the witness referred to it at page 413 of the Dokmanovic transcript. And it's a 112-page statement as she then recorded it as being, I think, if this is the statement with which we're concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, you've been given another part of the statement, Dr. Bosanac. Would you deal, first of all, with is said there. Is there anything you want to add to that as to why you wrote that about the JNA -- or about the colonel, rather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have this last page here in front of me, the last page of that statement of mine. I repeat, I wrote it under duress in prison and in the context of the entire situation, I mean the way I felt then. The truth is that Colonel Branko was correct towards me. He did not mistreat me physically or mentally, and that is what I wrote down. But what I saw in the camp is something quite different, except for the way Colonel Branko treated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave that aside, then. Could you please read out what you wrote. Could you read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By leave of the Judge, I can read it. As I said, this is a statement that was written in prison. "Colonel Branko, who talked to me and who analysed events with me, I would like to thank him sincerely for his humane approach and for instilling hope that there are people in the Yugoslav People's Army who want peace and humane co-existence among all the national groups in the area. He had an exceptional attitude towards me as a person and as a physician." I stated that and that is what I believe until the present day as far as Colonel Branko is concerned. However, unfortunately, Colonel Branko was one of the very few ones in the Yugoslav People's Army who behaved that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You have experience with him, but you don't have experience with others.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I do, Mr. Milosevic. I do have experience with others as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then we're going to get to these others. But we have to save time. So please tell me, in your statement, you talk about soldier Sasa Jovic, and that he, together with you, sought a cease-fire. He says that you always came to the room accompanied by two armed guards. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have here the interview that he gave. 20-year-old sergeant of the JNA, wounded after 17 days spent in an Ustasha environment, and he was brought to the Vukovar Hospital, and he became a patient of Dr. Bosanac, and her armed guards spent much more time by his sickbed than she did, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. brainwashing him with a pistol and a bomb. He said, "I saw Dr. Bosanac every day. She always came to our room accompanied by two armed guards." That is his interview. There are many other allegations made in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must bring these questions to a point. We can't go on in this way with you reading out long chunks. First of all, do you know, Dr. Bosanac, who the accused is talking about, a soldier called Sasa Jovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sasa Jovic. I know this soldier, Sasa Jovic. He was treated in hospital. He signed these appeals that I wrote aimed at a cease-fire. I don't know what interview this is and what kind of information Mr. Milosevic is referring to. I'm just claiming that this is incorrect. It is not correct that I was accompanied by armed soldiers when I went to patients' rooms. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that your colleague, Dr. Njavro Jure, also always went around accompanied by two armed men? Do you remember that he, for example, asked that Dr. Ivankovic resign? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You denied that the hospital was used as a location from which various weapons were used to shoot at the army. You denied that completely; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I denied it, because the hospital was not a military facility and there was no shooting done from there. However, every day the hospital was shelled by 90, 100 or more shells. That is a precedent. That is a war crime. However, there was no shooting from the hospital against the army because it was impossible to shoot from the army at army -- from the hospital at army positions that were three kilometres away. What you are saying is illogical and senseless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry that this seems illogical to you, but there are many witnesses who claim the opposite, the exact opposite, but their turn will come too. Mrs. Bosanac, according to the allegations made by your colleagues who worked together with you, they are ethnic Serbs, ethnic Croats, ethnic Hungarians, you not only denied the Serbs medical treatment, but some persons, according to your orders, were arrested, guarded in the basement of the hospital, or they were handed over to well-known torturers.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We'll deal with one thing at a time. The allegation is made that, first of all, that you denied Serbs medical treatment. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next allegation is that you ordered the arrest of some people and their guarding in the basement of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were there any prisoners in the basement of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Your colleague, I assume that you know him, Dr. Tomislav Djuranec, director of the medical centre in Borovo. Do you know that colleague of yours? I assume you do. You do, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 18th of December, 1991, he says, as a witness, that the ZNG brought him in because you personally ordered to have him brought to the police station. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says that you ordered the Croatian policemen to take him to the warehouse of the Borovo Kombinat and that he should not be allowed to go anywhere let alone go to the police station. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. It's not right. What you're saying is not right. If you wish, I can describe these events to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to describe anything.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying is not correct. What you're saying right now is not correct. Dr. Djuranec -- I mean, Dr. Djuranec probably wrote this under duress in prison because he was also in prison in Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can add anything you want about that doctor. Because of the seriousness of these allegations which are being made against you, you should have the opportunity to answer them. Now, is there anything you want to add about Dr. Djuranec? It's suggested you had him arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that that was not true. Dr. Djuranec was not under my authority at all. As director of the medical centre, he was in a completely different area. He was not under the Vukovar Medical Centre. He is a person who wanted to help in the entire situation. I heard that he was hiding some kind of medicaments and medical supplies, generally speaking, at the time when we did not have even the most basic supplies that were needed for treating the wounded. However, I did not talk to him, I did not talk to the police, nor do I have anything to do with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you aware, Doctor, that he was in fact arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard from some of these soldiers who came that he was brought in for interrogation because they found these medical supplies at his place. However, I personally do not know whether he had been arrested or what he had stated. I know that he was in camp, like I was, and I know that, during the exchange, he decided to remain on the other side. I also know that he was a very unhappy man because his son was killed during those days in the defence of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... his arrest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says - this is court transcript - "Dr. Vesna Bosanac, director of the Vukovar Hospital, accused me of having been inactive, of having hidden medical supplies for the Serbs who came to the shelter, that in April this year I gave oxygen to Dr. Jovic from Borovo Selo."

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not accuse him at all, nor do I know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says that he denied that, and he says: "During the conversation, they took me to Bosanac, and she ordered me to go to the warehouse in Borovo Kombinat and that I was not allowed to go anywhere. That is the direct order she gave to the military police that escorted me, and the military police took me from the Vukovar Hospital and handed me over to Kacusec, who was head in Borovo Selo of --"

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the way you're putting it. The fact is that he was in this shelter in the basement of Borovo Naselje, however, when -- as for his arrest and interrogation, I had nothing to do with that whatsoever, I had no idea about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about what it says further on in this court transcript: When he came to the rooms where they tortured him, where this Zdenko Stefancic was, next to the door, on the floor in that room, there was a stretcher and on that stretcher was Toma Gipsar from the Vukovar Hospital. He was wearing hospital pyjamas and he wore a hospital robe as well. He had been wounded. Why was he transferred from the Vukovar Hospital in pyjamas, in hospital pyjamas, to prison, Mrs. Bosanac? Was that on your orders or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Absolutely no one was transferred to any kind of prison on my orders. Tomo Jakovljevic, who had been wounded and who had had an amputation - he was wounded by a shell of the Yugoslav People's Army too - after having been treated for three weeks, after he had been given primary medical assistance, like all other wounded persons - every day there were about 15 to 20 of them - he was sent off to reserve hospitals and civilian shelters, and that is how he was sent to Borovokomerc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that this Toma Jakovljevic, in hospital pyjamas, was found by his own son? He was found dead. He was bullet-riddled in the chest.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Radivoje Jakovljevic, that is the son of the killed Jakovljevic, says that he had to run away from Vukovar because of the danger of him being liquidated. And on the 22nd of November in Borovo Naselje, near the kindergarten in the centre of Borovo Naselje, he found a heap where people were one over the other, and his father had been hit by a burst of gunfire in the chest and he was wearing a hospital bathrobe.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that because I did not hear about it. I did not see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could he have been taken out of hospital without your permission in order to be executed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. He was not taken out of hospital. He was sent from the hospital, together with 15 other wounded persons who had already been cured, to the reserve hospital of Borovokomerc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How he got killed and how he happened to be there is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, this Tomislav Djuranec - because this is what Mr. May was interested in yesterday - what he was in terms of his ethnic background, this first doctor who gave a statement, was Tomislav Djuranec by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think he's a Croat, but you'll have to ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he accuses you considerably. Are you claiming that his accusations levelled against you were made under duress, under pressure exerted by the investigating judge in the military court, or that there is a grain of truth in this, in what I've read out to you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not asserting anything as to how he stated that and under what kind of pressure, but I do know that I did not take part in anybody's arrest or is any of that correct, and I decisively deny that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Could this be admitted into evidence, this court transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This is the statement of a witness made to a military court. You are the first to object if any statement is put in uncross-examined and the same principle must apply to you as it does to the Prosecution, must it not? If you want to call that witness, you can do so in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the statement of this witness? Are you going to exhibit it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The statement of the -- the written statement of the witness that you referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a court transcript concerning the statement that this witness gave before a court of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're at cross-purposes. Wait a moment. We're talking now about the statement that Dr. Bosanac made in handwriting, which you referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement of Dr. Bosanac you mean. Of course you should have it exhibited. Of course I think it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. Now, have we got the entire statement? Have you got the entire statement there as opposed to merely part of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the entire --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot assess that because this is the first time I see this pile of paper. However, I repeat that I wrote this statement under very special circumstances, in prison, as a prisoner in a Serb camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Is this all that you have of that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. No. Precisely. That's what I'm trying to say. No, it's not. I have more here. I have three more pages. And I have to put a few questions in relation to that and then I'm going to give it to you, and that will be the entire statement then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would obviously first wish to have the whole statement; it will then organise its copying. And we would like to reserve our position on its admissibility when we've reviewed the entirety of the witness's answers in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just address us, if you would, on the statement which the witness has made that was being referred to the -- sorry. I want to make it plain. Deal with this in two ways: First of all, there is the statement which the accused has been cross-examining on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Inadmissible, for the usual reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you would explain the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Inadmissible for the usual reasons. Out of court statements are not ordinarily admissible. I think there's been one exception that we've recently encountered where there was a statement taken by ICTY investigators that the accused wanted to go in because it contained large numbers of matters of apparent detail in relation to the Dubrovnik shelling or fortifications, and that went in as an express exception to the general rule and practice of this Trial Chamber. All other rulings having been along the usual lines, statements relied on by the accused to make allegations are no more valuable as evidential material than the allegations themselves. They only become of value if and when they are attested to by the relevant witness as part of a defence case. So that these statements that the accused is cross-examining on, so he says, are within that general rule of exclusion. And if we make an exception for any of these statements, where will it end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. They're uncross-examined, and we have consistently refused the Prosecution admission of statements which have not been cross-examined where we are now having to consider admissibility under a particular Rule, Rule 92 bis. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's different -- and if it becomes relevant to consider applications to remit statements as part of the defence case in due course, they'll have to be considered then. This material simply should not be admitted. It has no evidential value or status and will simply burden the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Any statement made by this witness, of course, whether to an investigator or within proceedings at this court or elsewhere is capable of being used by the accused in cross-examination and it being exhibited as well as part of the material of this trial. It may be of great relevance if it contains inconsistencies and any other material within that statement. The position of statements made by other people who cite incidents with this witness and have made statements elsewhere in their dealings with this witness, which seem to be also some of the material that the accused is seeking to use, he's entitled to put those statements and ask the witness to deal with them and then he can make his own decision later on in the trial whether he wants to call the maker of that statement or who has commented about this witness, whether he wants to call then as a witness or not. But it would be appropriate for him to put such statements made by other people and give this witness the opportunity to deal with then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the statement itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The statement itself would generally not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It wouldn't be an exhibit because the author of it isn't here. But to have it as a piece of paper or document that you can look at to see what was being said is obviously a helpful aid in the trial process. But whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a rather complicated distinction, Mr. Kay, between an exhibit and something which is helpful to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just aiding to see where the questioner is going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think he's capable of putting his own questions, as he has done, from the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, he is, and he should be able to do that, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But that brings us back to the statement which is made by this witness in the circumstances which he's described. That, you say, is admissible as an exhibit in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, unless there's some reason why not, I think we would probably be minded to exhibit this statement. It looks as though it's all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it's all there, then let's get it copied and make it available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll exhibit the witness's statement. Let the witness have it back because the accused wants to ask one or two more questions about it. If you would do that and then hand in the other pages, then we'll finally exhibit it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you go on, Mr. Milosevic, I wanted to ask you, Doctor, about your relationship with Dr. Djuranec who made these accusations against you. In terms of the hospital hierarchy, you would have been senior to Dr. Djuranec?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djuranec did not work at the hospital at all. I was the director of the Vukovar Medical Centre, which comprised a hospital and primary health care clinic. There was another organisation, the Borovo health centre, of which Mr. Djuranec was the director.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. So you in fact had no working relationship with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So much the worse, as you accuse him of hiding medical supplies for the Serbs who came to the shelter, that you ordered him to go to the warehouse in Borovo Kombinat and not to move anywhere, that you ordered the police to arrest him and that the police took him from the Vukovar Hospital and handed him over to Ivica Kacusec, the commander in Borovo Naselje. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are saying has nothing to do with the truth. It's absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a statement.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be a statement, but what I'm saying is that what you have read out is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a court record on the questioning of this witness. I have no reason to tell falsehoods?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, will you exhibit this or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We've ruled on that. We're not exhibiting it. You've heard the reasons. It's a statement made out of court which we're not going to exhibit. You can call the witness. That's your remedy. Call Dr. Djuranec and we'll hear what he's got to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Toma Gipsar was an employee of your hospital, was he not, Mrs. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was taken from the hospital in hospital pyjamas and shot.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, he was retired. He was brought to the hospital as a wounded civilian, retiree - let me finish - who was operated on, and like other wounded patients whose condition had improved, he was taken to Borovo Naselje to the reserve shelter, because we received 90 new wounded every day. So we sent those whose condition had improved to civilian shelters. The shelter in Borovo Naselje was the best one. It had water, electricity, medical treatment was available there, and he was sent there from hospital. As for the other circumstances, how he was killed and what happened, I can say nothing about that because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people sent there so that, after that, the members of the National Guard Corps could take them out and shoot them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my view, they were not. I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His son who found him in hospital pyjamas also found his mother, also riddled with bullets.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about how they died or what happened. I know that his son - I heard this later - was on the Chetnik side and that he perpetrated various crimes against Croats, that he was connected with the murders in Velepromet and Ovcara, but that's just hearsay. I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He probably killed his own parents?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that Martin Sabljic was the commander in the collection centre where there were two and a half thousand people? Do you know that or don't you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a collection centre, it was a shelter in Borovo Naselje, where we organised a reserve hospital, where there were doctors, where the wounded and sick civilians were looked after. And this was not the only such shelter but it was the best one. There was another one in Naradnecki Dom [phoen], in Olajnice [phoen]. There were 12 such shelters that we organised to hide civilians and where we sent people who were ill or wounded but not seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Borovo Naselje, was Zdenko Stefancic interrogated? Do you know about Zdenko Stefancic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I'm hearing this name for the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly request that the speakers pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you hear that? A request, please, for both to pause after the question. Would you pause for the interpreters. Mr. Milosevic, bear it in mind too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you haven't heard of Zdenko Stefancic, am I to conclude that you did not hand these people over to Zdenko Stefancic who was sentenced to death because of the crimes he perpetrated there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard or saw or knew Zdenko Stefancic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mladen Ivankovic says that he complained to you when he was beaten by members of the National Guard Corps who cursed his Chetnik mother because he was a Serb. They slapped him. And you, as a colleague of his, replied that the people who were doing this were real heroes and that they were fighting for the homeland and that they had beaten him because they had found a cassette with Serbian songs on him.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume you also reject this record which refers to Dr. Mladen Ivankovic and his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. For the same reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that he wanted to escape from the hospital in the circumstances he was in and that you forbade him to leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't the only one. I forbade the whole staff from leaving the hospital for one single reason, and that was that shells were falling on the hospital and around it constantly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did this for his own safety?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Five people from the hospital had already been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the event?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was allowed to leave the hospital without my permission. The ambulances were not allowed to leave when they were to pick up the wounded, and the same applied to Dr. Ivankovic. It applied to everybody, because as soon as you left the hospital, you could be killed. They didn't know this because they were in the basement, but they could hear the shells falling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the event described by the chief of surgery, your colleague, when a Serb was brought in by the National Guard Corps, who had a head wound, and do you remember that, according to the testimony of this doctor, he was beaten in your hospital, and this young man behaved in a dignified way but they continued to beat him although he had been brought in as a wounded person?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely not true. Several wounded Serb soldiers were brought to our hospital, and they were all given the best possible medical treatment. We managed to cure many of them. There were some we were unable to save, unfortunately, but had anybody been -- or, rather, it is absolutely untrue that anybody was beaten or mistreated. What you are quoting is articles from Serbian newspapers. In 1997, when we returned to Vukovar, Dr. Ivankovic met us there and he told us that what the Serb newspapers were saying he had said was not true. If you wish, you can call him as a witness, but nobody was mistreated in the hospital because he was a Serb. Every wounded person was given the best possible treatment under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that this young man - and you say that he was not even beaten - was liquidated on that same evening and thrown into the Danube and that there is evidence to prove this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the man who was brought in by the ZNG and beaten.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody beat anyone in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, please answer yes or no and then you can say whatever you like, it's up to you. But is it true that it was you who tore out the page in the register saying that he had been admitted to hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who kept the records in the hospital testified to this.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not tear out any pages from the hospital register.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Nedeljko Turakalo, who was wounded in the leg and in the stomach, and who was treated by your fellow fighter, Dr. Njavro who intentionally allowed this man to bleed to death on the table and did not help him? Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Boban, who was 19 years old and also operated on by Njavro and who died during the operation? Because before this, other doctors had asked that he be operated on, but the operation was continually delayed, so that when it finally started, there was no hope for it to succeed. Do you remember this man Boban whom you also intentionally allowed to die?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Nobody intentionally allowed anybody to die. I personally do not remember Boban Gacic, but I know for a fact that all the wounded were treated in the same way and that nobody allowed anybody to die on purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that this man Sasa Jovic called General Raseta on the phone under duress?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. I asked him whether he wished to talk to him because I had told Raseta that in the hospital there were also soldiers of the JNA and that the hospital was being shelled every day, and he said he couldn't believe this, and I asked Sasa Jovic whether he wished to speak to him, and he said he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another colleague of yours, Djordje Kuzmanovic, said that on the 13th of November, soldier Ivica Nestorovic was brought to the hospital but that you personally refused him admission to the hospital but handed him over to the ZNG, and on that day that young man died and the members of the National Guard Corps burnt his corpse. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely untrue. Ivica Nestorov was never brought to the hospital for treatment. I cannot remember -- I know that I was asked about this when I was in the prison in Mitrovica. There was a soldier who was admitted to Borovo-Komerc, but because the tanks were blocking the way Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to the hospital, he couldn't be brought in. I think his name was Ivica Nestorov but I'm not sure. Dr. Emejdi might be able to confirm this because he worked in Borovo-Komerc. But this man never arrived in hospital, or at least, I don't remember. I think that was the man who was in Borovo. He couldn't have come because it was 12 days before the fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true -- is it true that the members of the JNA who were brought in, that television crews were also brought in to film them and that, after that, during the night, they disappeared, that when day broke their beds would be empty, that these people ended up in the Danube, as the nurses testified?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying absolutely never happened in Vukovar Hospital, ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how Branko Stankovic was killed? He was a patient in your hospital. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know that he was a patient either?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Let's move on, then. He was even filmed in a Croatian television programme. He was lightly wounded in the area below the knee but was killed after that. So you don't know about that either, do you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. And I have to say that in the Vukovar Hospital, from the 25th of August until the 20th of November, 2.250 wounded persons were admitted. Up until the 6th of November, we sent all these patients via computer and fax to the sanitary medical centre, and there is a complete record of all those patients, all those wounded people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, unfortunately, we have your own logbooks, your own records, your own statistics as to how many operations were performed, and I must say that the figures are far, far different from what you're claiming, but I don't want to waste time on that now.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be a good idea for you to hand over to this Tribunal all those documents that were taken away after the hospital had been occupied and is now at the medical military academy, and I can recommend to the Trial Chamber to ask for those records, the complete documents of the operations, the operations and surgery logbooks, and it would be a good thing if the Trial Chamber were to ask for those documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have to move on.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the real issues, Mr. Milosevic, because everything is written down in those records and documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, I think that everything should be undertaken to learn the truth.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be a good idea indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. All those documents and everything else, but unfortunately, it's quite contrary to what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just give up the documents and they'll see for themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I haven't got them.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could ask for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... this argument. Just one moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 17th of November, 1991, that is to say immediately prior to the entrance of the JNA, that Croatian guardsmen would come to the hospital, and members of MUP, to change their clothing, to put on civilian clothes and hospital clothes, that in this way 200 of them came in and tried to pull themselves out of the encirclement? Was that how it was or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not how it was. On the 17th of November, and it was a Sunday, the hospital was busy preparing itself for the evacuation. Records were being written out, discharge papers, and so on and so forth. That has nothing to do with these people changing their clothes. Nothing of that nature happened in hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you say no, and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say no, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that a number of rifles in the X-ray room were stored, that quite a lot of rifles were stored in the X-ray room. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that in those days before the JNA arrived, that the hospital was generally used for storing weapons? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not permit that, nor do I have any knowledge as to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man who was nicknamed Srna or Do who came to the hospital and asked that all the soldiers be killed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that man, but he did not ask that all the soldiers be killed. At least, he didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did he ask for individual soldiers to be killed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't ask me anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Is it true that, together with Dr. Njavro - because you and Njavro were actually at the head of all this business - that you prepared medical documents where you listed as dead in those documents and records members of the Croatian National Guard Corps who were well known for the crimes they had committed in Vukovar in order to protect them from the long arm of the law? Is that true? And your colleagues say that it is.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the number of death certificates issued and ID papers of guardsmen who were not dead but in fact are still living, who are alive?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that on the night before the surrender, and this is something that eyewitnesses have told us, have testified about, that they saw these Croatian National Guards Corps members taking off their uniforms, putting on civilian clothing, pretending to be staff of the hospital. Many of them put plaster casts on their arms to make them appear as having been injured. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. And the hospital wasn't turned over. What was happening was an evacuation organised by the International Red Cross which wasn't conducted in the fashion it should have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the person who suggested to the Croatian National Guard Corps members to come to the hospital, take off their uniforms, and put on civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Skokic Miroslav, a member of the Croatian National Guard Corps, who on the 9th of May made a statement as a witness, says in his statement that he was mobilised on the 1st of October, 1991 and that in the general chaos and noise that was going on in one of the halls where they were mobilised, that you yourself appeared, and he says you said, and he quotes you: "Who wants to go to the breakthrough and does not wish to surrender can go behind the municipality building. Those of you who wish to remain can go to the hospital with you where they will change their clothes, be given a white hospital coat, and be included in a unit to cater to the needs of the hospital." Is that something that is not true?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what that's about. It's not true. I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did anything like this happen? This is a very broad allegation which the accused is making, that they were -- members of the defence, essentially, were masquerading as patients. Although I must say what the relevance of that, even if it is true, is. I don't know how that can justify what happened to those men being taken over and shot and executed in the way they were, over 200 [Realtime transcript read in error "2006"] of them, I don't know. But since accused is asking it, did anything like this happen at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the accused has asked me to do, to link this up with the name of this man Skokic, I don't know who the man is, but this is what the situation was like with the hospital: There was group of guardsmen, guards, who, from Jastreb, were ordered to provide security for the hospital. These were eight men led by a man called Tihomir Perkovic. They were in charge of providing safety and security for the hospital, for ensuring that food could be brought in and medical supplies, logistic support, things of that kind. And it is these men who were in the hospital when the evacuation was being organised. And some of them were found at Ovcara as well. Under what circumstances, I don't know, and I don't know whether they've all been identified either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification. There is a mistake in the transcript. I did not refer to 2006 being executed. The figure was over 200, as I referred to it. Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm interested in, Mr. May, is whether you have already taken up your positions and -- with respect to this case, and that is how I'm to take your explanations, just in the way you asked the witness yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. No. I'm merely -- and I'm going to interrupt you because that's a totally improper observation. I'm merely asking the witness to clarify her evidence. If you wish to clarify your position as to the relevance of these questions, you can do so. What I questioned is the relevance of whether there were guardsmen dressed in civilian clothes and patients there or not. Now, you can explain to us, if you will, what the relevance of this is, if it in any way, you are saying, justifies -- just a moment -- justifies what happened afterwards when these people were taken out and executed at Ovcara, because that's the essential matter that we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the relevance of it lies in the fact that the greatest criminals were allowed to take refuge there; criminals who had perpetrated the most violent crimes. So when you talk about the defenders of Vukovar in line with your assumed positions, these were in fact criminals who had perpetrated crimes in Vukovar. That's the first point. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How does that compare to what happened at Ovcara, even if it's right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, as far as I'm concerned, none of this is relevant, because from the information and facts I have, which I assume are available to you too, Serbia has nothing to do with Ovcara, and I was the president of Serbia. And I'm trying to explain here that the JNA had nothing to do with Ovcara either, because the JNA enabled the evacuation to take place of thousands of people from there. And I'm sure you'll remember, Mrs. Bosanac, the evacuation from Vukovar right down to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, one thing you have to understand is that it's not a defence to attack the other side. Now, I know, because it's quite clear, that it is part of your strategy to do so, simply to attack the Croats, but what you have to do understand, the war crime and the crime with which you are charged with which this indictment deals is concerned with what happened at Ovcara, and that is essentially what this part of the evidence is about, leading up to. Now, you choose to spend your time attacking the other side, but we need to know what your defence is in relation to these particular incidents and these killings. Now, if you've got relevant questions as to that, of course we'll listen to them. But merely listening to you attacking the other side is of no assistance to us. The witness has answered. She said, as far as she is concerned, there were not criminals or anybody else dressed up as patients. Now, she's answered that. You insist on going on, and it seems to me you're wasting of the time of the Court. It's quite plain that she's given her answer and nothing more can really be said about it. Why don't you move on in the time which available to you, which is now limited, and deal with the incidents at Ovcara. If you have got a case that you want to put in relation to it, of course we'll hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be so kind as to tell me, Mr. May, as a professional and legal man yourself, to explain to me this: Do I have to prove that I have nothing to do with Ovcara or do those people who - I didn't even know about this title - those who claim that I have something to do with that, that the weight of proving it -- the burden of proof is on them, they have to show that I did have something to do with that and that all these accusations against the Serbs are true? Do I have to prove that is not true or is the burden of proof on them, those people who are claiming that the Serbs perpetrated the crimes, should show that they did indeed commit them? So where does the burden of proof lie, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me add something this time. Your case may be this, that JNA tried to sort out some war criminals or some Serb forces from the Croat patients or among patients, but you don't have -- when the witness denies that, you don't have to put every detail to the witness. Later, you can call the witness who can give evidence about that. At that time, the Court will decide what the truth was and what weight is to be given to every witness. So move on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon. I'm not claiming -- the point isn't in the fact whether the JNA tried to find the perpetrators. The point is that hiding this conspiracy in crime and that they are trying to conceal the perpetrators of the most grievous crimes and therefore, conspiracy in those crimes. And of course we're talking about withholding medical treatment and aid to Serbs, and it also includes the killings, some of which I have mentioned here, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Precisely my point. How much further does that take us, apart from your putting a negative case against the witness? What you should be doing is concentrating on a positive case. You have to prove nothing. But if you have a case, as you claim to, about the JNA not being involved, then you should put it to the witness so that she can hear. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, is it true that at the time when you realised that there was the danger of you being held accountable and responsible precisely for the crimes you committed, that you started to disclose, to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. uncover who belong -- within the JNA, who belongs to the hospital staff and who belongs to the Croatian National Guard Corps, that you started telling the JNA members who these people were?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true at all. I had nothing to disclose. I uncovered nothing. All this is incorrect and that I withheld medical assistance to anybody. I gave medical assistance to everybody, and there is a lot of proof to bear that out, both among the Serbs and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know about the evacuation -- and I think it was called something like exchange, actually. It was no kind of exchange when you had hundreds of buses from Vukovar going via Bijeljina to Dvor and then towards Brcko and so on, to be turned over to the Croatian authorities; soldiers, civilians, wounded persons, et cetera. Do you know about this massive column organised by the army to turn these people over to safety over there? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was in prison in Serbia, but I do know that at that time, in the space of two days, from the hospital towards Sremska Mitrovica, 174 wounded persons were transported, and that's what we did. We started looking for the rest, because there were 260 unaccounted for, that were missing. And we found 200 of them killed at Ovcara, of that figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never heard of the great large convoy which had to cross over into Bosnia because of the shooting coming from the other side, to stop in Vorovi [phoen] and then move on to Brcko so that these people could be handed over to the Croatian authorities ultimately? An enormous number of people. Do you know about this long convoy and its advance?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. They were women, children, the wounded, some hospital staff and some civilians. Most of the people of Vukovar, 5.666, in fact, stayed in camps in Serbia. You say that you have nothing to do with Vukovar. Well, in those camps in Serbia, people were beaten up and destroyed to the tune of 5.666 persons. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, I'd just like to focus on what you were saying yesterday. You mentioned my name in one context and said you wanted to ask Mr. Milosevic to release the people. This is the first time I heard about that. Now, is it clear to you - and you were in a military prison, you were under the competence of the military authorities - that all those people were not either de jure or de facto under the competence of Serbian organs but they came under the competence and authority of the organs of the Yugoslav People's Army, just like you yourself did. The Yugoslav People's Army is not an organ of Serbia but is an organ of Yugoslavia, and not a single one of those prisoners of yours who were taken off to the various collection centres came under the competence and authority of Serbia and Serbian organs. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't know whether this is the time or the place for us to remind ourselves of certain things, and those are that at that time, the person who was the ideological motive force of everything was you yourself and that you allowed the international community, on the 18th, as was agreed upon, to enter Vukovar, that you called up Slijvancanin on the phone. Had you done that, there wouldn't have been any persons killed. Enough people were killed by the shelling. That is a war crime too. 1.300 people were killed by the shells that fell. But had you allowed the international community to come from Belgrade and enter Vukovar with Cyrus Vance -- we saw them enter the hospital and had they stayed there, had they remained there, Ovcara would never have happened and the camps would never have happened. But it was your objective for the camps to happen and for Ovcara to happen in order to prove and show that Vukovar, now half of Croatia, was Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine, Mrs. Bosanac. I see that you have learnt your lesson in history very well, but doesn't it seem to you that the ideological leader of that crime and that awful war and those awful crimes against Vukovar was the same consciousness and awareness which prevailed in the 1940s of the last century and brought the whole of mankind before an abyss?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now going a long way from the indictment. We'll get back to it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ideological leaders of the conflict are those who were trying to break up Yugoslavia, Mrs. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is a long way from the witness's evidence. Now, unless you've got anything further to put, time will be running out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This other convoy, the one that you refer to just now, you said by Sremska Mitrovica, 140 something, how many thousands were in this other convoy?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were expelled from Vukovar. 22.360 persons were expelled from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that those who were evacuated in the presence of the European Monitors, the International Red Cross, in order to have aid given to them, that they were expelled there and that the JNA was actually expelling these people by sending them off to safe areas? Is that your claim?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It carried out --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was ethnic cleansing on your instructions. You should have allowed the international community to come in. In October, when Vance first came to Yugoslavia, to the then Yugoslavia, he should have been allowed to go to Vukovar and then he should have frozen things where they were, and then there would not have been any killings. At least, Vukovar was half destroyed. However, your objective was to kill, to destroy, to cleanse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's not go into all this senseless stuff, what whose objective was. We're going to get to that when we move on to serious matters. Tell me, how did you get this idea at all that the JNA had something to do with Ovcara when the JNA got all these people out of there and sent them to a safe area? Of course some were sent to prison if they were suspects of criminal action, such as you were.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said now is not true, but as far as I'm concerned, the Yugoslav army is responsible because Major Sljivancanin entered the hospital on the 20th in the morning. He brought in officers of the Military Academy, Medical Academy, doctors from there, and he said, "Dr. Bosanac, you are no longer in charge. Now the hospital is under the Military Medical Academy of the JNA." After that, the wounded persons were taken to Ovcara and killed there. So as far as I'm concerned, it is Major Sljivancanin and the Military Medical Academy that are responsible for that crime. They allowed the wounded to be executed at Ovcara. My father-in-law, an old man, a sick man, he was executed there. He was killed by an exit/entry wound in the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's not go into all the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are important details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nobody is justifying the execution of people, regardless of whether they are civilians or soldiers. It can even be a soldier, a captured soldier. But a captured soldier is a prisoner of war and it is a crime to commit -- to kill a person like that. I'm just trying to clarify that this was not done by the JNA. And I'm trying to say that it's your local conflicts there and the hatred that you fanned at the time when this new leadership came to the helm of Croatia. But we're going to get to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can answer that question. Again, the accused asserts that it was not done by the JNA. From your knowledge, the JNA were present at the hospital, is that what you say, and involved, having entered the hospital, in the patients being taken out. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the 19th of November, 1991, they entered the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but just so that we can clarify the position and shorten matters, but beyond that, of course, you can't give evidence because you were in fact detained yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But in the morning of the 20th, I was there at 7.00 a.m. when Major Sljivancanin said I was no longer in charge of the hospital, it was the Military Medical Academy that was in charge of the hospital from then on. That was on the 20th in the morning at 7.00 a.m. At 10.00, the wounded were taken out and taken to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What? Are you trying to say that the Military Medical Academy took the wounded out and killed them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The Military Medical Academy and Major Sljivancanin took over the hospital. They are responsible. As to who killed them, that is something that I cannot say because I was not there, however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're not going to take the matter much further with this argument. We've heard the witness's evidence and as far as she can take it. It will be a matter for us to judge what happened thereafter on the basis of any other evidence we hear. We will adjourn now. It's a little before time, but -- Mr. Milosevic, you've got a quarter of an hour left. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, Mr. May, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We seem to have lost quite a lot of time over the explanations, or your explanations as to procedural matters, and so I think that it would be in order if you were to extend the time I have allotted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in any event, I was mistaken. You've got rather longer even on our own interpretation. I said you can have two hours in all. You've had nearly an hour and a half. So you've got half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, before I continue, let me clarify something. I had the impression that you were not wearing your headset when I put the question of the extension of time in connection with the time lost because of procedural clarifications. You said half an hour, but that's in accordance with what you said yesterday. However, now there are a number of procedural explanations which have taken up time, so could you extend this time of half an hour for this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see how we get on and we'll have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll try to expedite matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, you were not present in Vukovar when the civilian authorities took over control of Vukovar and the surrounding area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what civilian authorities you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The civilian authorities established there then.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? Can you tell me the date?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the fall of Vukovar. I don't know the exact date, but the civilian authorities then took control of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, 1991, I was taken to prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's just what I'm getting at. So you weren't there when the civilian authorities took over Vukovar. Very well. Is it correct that, after you were appointed head of the hospital, you established a war staff, a Crisis Staff where you and Njavro and several other people were members?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that when I was appointed head of the hospital I accepted this post if the people who had previously carried out important duties would help me. This was in accordance with instructions received from the Ministry of Health. And in this Crisis Staff, there was Dr. Mladen Ivankovic, Dr. Djordje Kuzmanovic, Dr. Leopold Kerek, Mr. Njegovan Krstic. That was the Crisis Staff I set up, and the head nurse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have the decision here on the setting up of the Crisis Staff, and it says Dr. Vesna Bosanac, Leopold Kerek, Mladen Ivankovic, Njegovan Krstic, Lipovcevic Danijel, Amalija Salaj, Miroslav Lipovcevic, Jozefina Ceric, Dr. Ivica Matus, and Dr. Tomo Prgic. As we can see, there was one Serb in the Crisis Staff, Mladen Ivankovic.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
