utterances.text: That's not true. There was more than one Serb. If you want to count, we can take the names one by one. I'll tell you what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you, because as far as I know, you dismissed most of the Serbs that held important posts.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. No Serbs were removed from their posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the director of the hospital was replaced and you were appointed in his stead.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Popovic resigned of his own free will, and I was elected by the workers' council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying that Dr. Popovic resigned of his own free will and that you were elected by the workers' council?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I have the original document here, and I ask that it be looked after properly, because it is truly an original and not a photocopy. It's addressed to the medical centre from the president of the workers' council in Vukovar, asking Dr. Rade Popovic to be relieved of his duty. And it's signed by the minister, Professor Dr. Andrija Hebrang, the Minister of Health of Croatia, and the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar is to be informed of this. Would you look at this. This is not a resignation. It's a demand that he be relieved of his duty by the Minister of Health. You can look at this document --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can look at it, but I have never seen it before in my whole life. As you yourself say, this document was forwarded to the Municipal Assembly. I heard about it but I've never seen it. Regardless of this, Dr. Popovic did resign. If you wish, you can call him as a witness and he will tell you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this an original document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say, because I'm looking at it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it say, "Request for relieving the head of the hospital of his duty"?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says, but it's addressed to the president of the workers' council, and I reiterate that I have never seen this document before now. It was probably addressed to Dr. Stanimirovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want that exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an original document, Mr. May, and as for what Mr. Nice said that an exception was made, let me remind you that when a protected witness from Western Slavonia, a functionary from Western Slavonia was interrogated here, you admitted notes from police stations because the standpoint taken was that these were issued by state authorities. Now we are dealing not with police stations but with court records, and you rejected them as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've dealt with that. We'll exhibit this document. Give it the next number, please. Yes. The registrar reminds me we've get the Resolutions outstanding. This document obviously must be translated before it's finally admitted but we'll give it the next exhibit number after the Resolutions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that, in a letter of the 13th of October, 1991, according to my information, you personally wrote a letter to Granic, the Deputy Prime Minister, and you say if any vehicle, including an ambulance, leaves the barracks, you will consider it an aggression on the defence line, and every vehicle on every barrack will be destroyed. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as it's not correct --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as you don't know what I'm talking about, Mrs. Bosanac, here is a document written in your own handwriting, addressed to Mr. Granic, the Deputy Prime Minister, about the expected evacuation, and you are saying what is in the barracks of the JNA, full of reservists and Chetniks, and in case a single vehicle, including an ambulance, leaves the barracks, we will consider it an aggression against the front line and every vehicle and the barracks will be destroyed. The head of the medical centre Vukovar, Vesna Bosanac. It's your own handwriting. It's a letter written in your own hand. Will you look at it.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may refer to the circumstances surrounding the organisation of the convoy of Medecins sans Frontieres who were come to the Vukovar Hospital on the 12th of October --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before going any further, the witness should see the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say: "If any vehicle, including an ambulance, leaves the barracks, we will consider it an aggression against the front line and every vehicle and the barracks will be destroyed." You, as the head of the hospital, wrote this to the Deputy Prime Minister. Is this your letter?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my letter, and it is not my handwriting. I'm seeing this for the first time now. I don't know who wrote this. As you can see from my earlier letters, this is not my handwriting at all nor is this my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This can be checked, because it does say, "Vesna Bosanac, head --"

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, but anybody could have written this letter. On this paper, I see it says Borovo. I never used this kind of letterhead. And I don't know who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you wrote official letters, you typed them out or, rather, you wrote it in capital letters?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't write in capital letters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This can be easily checked.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It's not my handwriting, and I didn't write it. I don't know who could have written this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we have in mind for this document is to mark it for identification, not to admit it at the moment since the witness denies writing it. The Prosecution can, of course, see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. An immediate point before I sit down is would the accused perhaps provide the best original he has. He may have the original. We know he's got one other original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification. If you've got the original, Mr. Milosevic - you hear the point Mr. Nice makes - we'll have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were questioned on the 9th of December --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but not for the first time, when procedural matters are raised that it appears not to suit the accused's convenience to answer, he declines to answer them. Now, he is engaging in this trial, whether he likes to admit it or not, and if the Bench asks him if he has an original, I would respectfully invite the Court to require him to answer. Because where a document is raised that may be a forgery, it is vitally important that the relevant parties - which is the Court and the Prosecution - have the earliest access to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since the question was put on the basis if he had the original he was to produce it, I thought his answer was plain. But, Mr. Milosevic, let's make sure of this. Do you have the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have given you what I have, and I will check whether the original is available to my associates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have given you what I have received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 9th of December, 1991, you were questioned and explained in the presence of counsel that you contacted Mile Dedakovic Jastreb, and you mentioned him awhile ago. You said that he put sentries around the hospital. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of the crimes that Dedakovic perpetrated throughout the long period of time over the Serbian population and Serbian civilians in Vukovar? I'm referring to Mile Dedakovic Jastreb.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any crimes perpetrated by Mile Dedakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Did you have information about the number of Serbs in collection centres? Let me mention only the one led by Marin Sabljic, who himself confessed to the most serious crimes that he perpetrated in Vukovar. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of any collection centres. As I have said, there were civilian shelters where all people took refuge. There were sick people, elderly people of all ethnic backgrounds. I don't know of any collection centres in Vukovar. I don't know what you mean by "collection centre."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have here a handwritten statement, a statement made by Martin Sabljic, born in 1939, and so on and so forth, in connection with the truth about the events in the Komerc, Novo Obucarna Kombinat, Borovo shelter. And he talks about the military police or, rather, the National Guard Corps giving him the task of commanding the civilian shelter. He says that the number of people in the shelter constantly increased.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you're putting this to me. I know nothing about this. I knew Martin Sabljic. He was killed in a traffic accident. I don't know exactly when. I did know him. I know that he was in the camp and that he made many statements under duress, but I don't know what he said, and I have no idea. I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says that the number of people there grew day by day, that records were kept by a girl whose last name was Levantic, he didn't know her first name, and she gave the information to Lavoslav Bosanac. That's your husband, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lavoslav Bosanac is my husband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he goes on to explain that the policeman who asked him whether he was the commander of the shelter asked for the logbook recording the citizens who were there, put his pistol on the table, banged his fist on the table, and said, "In two minutes, I'm giving you two minutes to bring me some young males. I don't care who I kill, and you're not going to hide the people in here," and then he speaks of killing.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you're putting this to me. I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there's no point putting this to the witness unless she knows something about it. She knows nothing about this shelter. She said so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, she knows because he says that this information was passed on to her husband. So I assume she knew something about it. Do you wish to admit this statement or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume you don't. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I can't find it here, but do you know that your husband received money from these members of the National Guard Corps for these activities?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is absolutely untrue. I'm certain he didn't receive any money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, while Mr. Milosevic is looking for his questions, was your husband also called as Lav?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lav, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where did he work at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a civil engineer, and he was employed in the Borovo factory. During the war, they were also working as much as they could. They repaired what had been destroyed. For example, the bakery, which had been hit by a shell and was set fire to, they repaired that for them to be able to bake bread. And then they had this civil engineering unit which was operational to ensure electricity supplies and water supplies for the hospital and for the civilian shelters. And it's true that his office was in the Komerc shelter where there was a large hall, well supplied with electricity and water, and there were almost a thousand people there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have here the original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. In Borovo Naselje --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- was there a time when Major Sljivancanin had asked you to write a letter to your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Major Sljivancanin came to the hospital, I warned him and said that there was a reserve hospital there and that the injured should be evacuated there. But this took place in quite a different way. The Novi Sad Corps had taken control of it, and this large building of Borovokomerc - and you can see a photograph of it in my book - on the 19th it was occupied, taken over by tanks. The tanks targeted it until it was completely destroyed, until it lay in ruins, and then they used incendiary bombs which they threw into the shelter and so that the patients and the wounded and the staff who were there were almost -- almost suffocated. Any husband left with -- waving a white flag. He asked them to stop killing people, and they kept up this tank attack for six hours, until they had completely destroyed the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was whether Major Sljivancanin asked you to write a letter to your husband. You can say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you claim that your husband did not receive money from the Croatian National Guard Corps, I have a payout slip here, the original one from the payout slip block, and it was seized by them. I will supply you with the original and keep a copy for myself. And it says 1 million 100 thousand to be paid out to Lav Bosanac, and the signature of your husband on the 16th of October, 1991, that he received the money.. You can take a look at that payout slip and tell us whether this is indeed the signature of your husband, because you said a moment ago that he never received any money whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer that question? May I answer Mr. Milosevic, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you can. Have a look at the -- have a look at the document you're being shown and you can answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this document it, says payout slip number 31/91, 1.110.000 dinars, Bosanac Lavoslav, payment for Borovo, in Vukovar on the 16th of October, 1991. In this way, the social accounting service of the day or, rather, the bank paid out sums of money to all the employees of the Borovo factory, and my husband was the superior to the civil engineers and the civilian logistics group, and I can only assume -- and this is the signature of my husband. I can only assume that this was a sum of money paid for their salaries. It was paid to his civil engineering group, and it says down here: "For payments for Borovo."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to have that tendered into evidence, because this has not been challenged. This is a payout slip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is a payout slip.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The payout slip has been signed and the witness has confirmed that it is her husband's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you'd have to ask him, but the signature is similar to my husband's signature, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It will bear the next number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about Count Elc castle. Do you know that that cultural and historical movement was used as the ZNG storage house and that it was a vantage point from which they opened fire at the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know about the museum, about Count Elc museum is the following: That in mid-August, 1991, part of the castle was completely destroyed, and the people who were there, who worked there, were hit by the shells. One of my fellow doctors, Sinisa Telarevic went to intervene but he was hit by a shell. Actually, the ambulance he was in was hit by a shell. The palace museum was destroyed, like Vukovar itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I have an addition to Vesna Bosanac's statement, once again written in your own handwriting. During the war between the 8th and the 11th, you speak about the bullets and you say: "The guards I think had a warehouse of their own and some premises there. I established that in August when I was in -- when I asked the chief staff of the Croatian medical corps, army medical corps, that's when they informed me of that. And then after helping out with medical supplies, I was allegedly sent two truckloads, whereas nothing actually arrived." And then you have a picture here, or diagram, showing what it looked like, what was to be found in the gardens, palace gardens, the TO, the municipality, et cetera; the rifles, the scaffolding where the guards were. So these were all diagrams and sketches that you drew?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll let you have a look in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go on, then. Let me see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to speak about the secondary school and say that there was a ZNG base in the secondary school itself.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is your question in this respect?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Count Elc palace and the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you mentioned a secondary school. What do you want to know about that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have a base both in Count Elc palace, which was a cultural monument in itself, and in the secondary school building which was a health institution?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war I was neither in the palace or in the gymnasium, the secondary school building. But let me mention that when you say secondary school, it wasn't a health institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I meant educational institution.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you heard that the ZNG had its warehouse in the gymnasium, in the secondary school building.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, but I didn't actually see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You didn't see it. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in due course the witness should see what it is you are quoting from, and then we will have the statement exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an addition to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell us, please, is that the addition you yourself made, and is it written in your own handwriting by you yourself? And the sketches too, where the Croatian National Guard Corps had its base and so on.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an addition to my statement. And like the previous statement, I wrote it out while I was in custody in Sremska Mitrovica under the conditions that prevailed there, under duress. This is my handwriting, and I did indeed write this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make the sketches too?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me have a look. I'm not quite sure. Yes, these are my sketches. Let me just take a look at them, what else you've attached here. Yes. That is the addition to my statement that I wrote out while I was in custody in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I don't suppose you're challenging that the guard had its base in Elc palace and in the secondary school building.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know. I heard about it but I didn't actually see for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think that you wrote down these facts here, which means that both secondary school and the palace were turned into military targets, just like your hospital from which there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, Mr. Milosevic. Don't say that. That's not true. I wrote here that I had heard there were guards there, but that has nothing to do with the hospital, and there is no justification in the eyes of the world and before the public that the hospital was destroyed by shells on a daily basis, and there's no justification for that having been so. I don't see that you can't understand that. You don't want to understand it, but that's your problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I wish to establish is whether it was a military target or not.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital was not a military target in any way. It displayed the Red Cross emblem at two points. People were treated there of all ethnicities, and we treated them as best we could. And we couldn't do any better because you yourself organised the blockade of Vukovar, and you targeted the hospital with shells every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. Dr. Bosanac, if you would mind not personalising this for the moment. Mr. Milosevic, we've decided that you will have 40 minutes in all in this session, which means you've got another ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I'll have to skip a great many questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that statement of yours, did you write in your very own hand that you heard about corpses that were floating on the Danube River and that you will not eat fish from the Danube for a long, long time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I can't remember exactly what I said because it's a 16-page statement. That's what it says there, but that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put a question to you about the killing of patients from your hospital, inter alia those who were thrown into the Danube after that.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. And that is not correct that patients from my hospital were being killed. No one was killed from my hospital, and no one was thrown into the Danube.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not killed in the hospital itself, but they were killed out of that hospital. I gave you a few examples.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you once again that I have no knowledge of this whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that there were ramps from launching pads for rockets that were fired against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that, because I would have seen that or heard about that. There were no launching pads as far as I know. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the chapel of the castle? Was that the centre for killing Serbs after interrogation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that everywhere around the castle there were mortars and machine-gun nests from which --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I pass by often, and I never saw anyone shooting from there ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at the castle chapel people were electrocuted and then thrown into the Danube?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The chapel of Elc castle, I know where it was, and right next to it a grave was dug, and that is where we buried people who were killed by shells, and I drew that in these sketches of mine. And nobody killed anyone over there. There was no electricity, to begin with, and nobody killed anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even your Marin Vidic says in his statement that civilians were taken to the Danube, killed there, and then thrown into the Danube.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Marin Vidic says is something I don't know. I just know that he was in the camp himself and that he was also tortured and perhaps he gave statements under duress. I personally do not know what he stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you wrote in your own statement, and that is what you read here, that you were not under torture. On the contrary, that you were treated very humanely, attentively --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've already been over that. You've drawn that to our attention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, she said that he was also under torture. I mean, as if she had been under torture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She didn't. The two cases are quite different. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that when talking to the monitors of the ECMM when you were arrested, you said that the JNA carried out the evacuation in a correct manner and that the representatives of Croatia did not have any objections whatsoever, and you made no comments with regard to that? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have stated that when I was arrested. I did not know what the evacuation looked like at all at the time. I know about it now. I heard about it later. But when I was arrested, I did not have any idea as to how the evacuation took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you asked the International Red Cross to be present during evacuation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you want, under the protection of the Red Cross, to actually evade responsibility for the crimes you had committed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question is really an exaggeration. I did not commit any crimes, and there is nothing that I should evade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you then called "Mengele"?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then you have to ask your very own journalists who, on your instructions, said all this nonsense. This is total nonsense, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you entered the names of about 150 guardsmen in the lists of persons who were to be evacuated from the hospital, those who committed crimes in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. The list of evacuation includes the names and surnames of wounded and sick persons with accompanying diagnoses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Colonel Mrksic sent you food and water on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in Vukovar 1.100 persons were killed, in your auxiliary statements attached to your statement. But in your statement before the court in Belgrade, you said that 520 dead persons were brought to the hospital out of which 158 belonged to the ZNG and 60 to the MUP, eight children, and the rest were civilians, however, you did not know how each and every person lost their lives; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at one point in time. I don't know exactly which date it was. And I know how people lost their lives. They were all killed by shells and bombs of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is your additional statement, and what I quoted a minute ago is in there where you say 520 persons, out of which 158 were members of the ZNG and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 520 civilians. That was the total of people who were killed by shells of the JNA. 1.150, as far as I know. Four hundred persons are still missing. We don't know how and where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is exactly what you say. So you cannot claim that they were killed with shells, and now you say that you don't know how they lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed by shells and bombs. They were killed by shells and bombs, those who were brought to hospital. It was quite obvious. There is accompanying documentation but you and Belgrade have this documentation. It would be a good thing, for the sake of justice, to have this documentation handed over here to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you compile a list of persons from the ZNG who were killed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official list of persons killed from the National Guards Corps and from the police was compiled by Branko Lukenda and Tomislav Hegedus. They are considered to be missing until the present day, and they were arrested on the evening of the 19th by the Yugoslav People's Army. I kept records in a little book so that I would have information if somebody asked me about the number of persons who were dead. But this was not official. Officially, it was compiled by these representatives of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a list from your medical centre and it says here, "Killed from the 25th of August onwards, active force of the National Guards Corps." I don't know why one name is circled and others are not. And then the MUP, the medical centre Vukovar, the list of persons killed in this fighting. So you can take this as well as the additional statement so that we don't waste any time.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably the list that I sent along with the appeals that I included in the book on a specific date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not very tidy.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the list that was compiled by my secretary. However -- yes, this is what it says here. "Killed persons from the 25th of August." But I don't see up to what date, because unfortunately, these lists grew longer and longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 5 of your statement, you say that the Municipal Staff decided not to bury the dead at the old cemetery. Who passed that decision and why?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the old cemetery, which is very close to the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army, the dead were buried already in the month of September. But so many shells were falling on that cemetery that burials became risky for the persons who were actually doing the burying. Therefore, the municipal Crisis Staff passed a decision to stop burials at that cemetery. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is now up, but you can ask two more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, unfortunately, I have -- I have hundreds of other questions, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Two more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then let me go back to the statement. There are a few more remaining pages of that big statement. You said that it was peaceful in Vukovar, and in the statement, you say quite decidedly -- you talk about mining shops, torching shops, those that were owned by Serbs, and you say, "I, as many other citizens, were unpleasantly surprised when we found out that every four to five days a Serb restaurant would be blown up," and you talk about Vukovar, Borovo Naselje, about violent acts that were committed then. Is that right or is that not right? Because you say that, before these events took place, it was peaceful in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was peaceful. After Borovo Selo, when 12 policemen were killed, I heard that a Serb cafe was blown up or, rather, it was set on fire, but we don't know how. But I don't know why you're asking me about that. I have no information about that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you because you say that you heard that every four or five days something was being blown up.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I cannot say that. But Mr. Milosevic, I really don't know why you're asking me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you wrote it down in your very own statement. So please take the remaining three pages.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can go on discussing my statement for another hundred days, but that's not important. The important thing is that had you not brought in Chetniks to Borovo Selo, we would have had peace. We had a parliamentary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Doctor, I realise that you feel provoked, but please just restrict your answers to the questions. Now, your last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said to you that I had hundreds of questions left, but now during the break I got excerpts -- now during the break, I got excerpts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now during the break, I got the excerpts that you referred to from the books of anaesthesiology from your hospital from the end of November, and it is quite clear that you did not carry out 750 surgeries during that period, the way you had put it, as you have asserted, but only 187. Why did you give this false information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all, let the witness see the document. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no idea what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness see the document which you're relying on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the last page is the first one and the first one is the last one. I mean, it goes backwards. And it starts from June and it ends at the end of November.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the protocols, as far as I can see now, although I would have to have a closer look at it. This is one of the protocols that come from the nurse at anaesthesiology. This is not a relevant document. This is a protocol that gives a list of some persons only. The real documentation says otherwise. There is a description of the operation involved, there is a signature of the main surgeon and then of the anaesthesiologist. This is just a very superficial record. However, as for the complete medical records, I mean because records were kept in five ways of patients at the Vukovar Hospital, all of these records were taken away by the Yugoslav army. So it would be a good thing, for humanitarian reasons, for you to return these records so that people could evaluate their disabilities and so that people who survived could be assisted, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will admit that. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to note, Mr. May, that with regard to each and every question, I quoted the relevant documents of the state institutions in charge. So I believe that all these documents should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Bosanac -- Dr. Bosanac, first of all, I would like to put the following question to you: When you were exchanged in the month of December, at that time, was that exchange carried out disregarding the fact of who was suspected of having done what? Was the exchange of persons conducted complete then? A number Croats were exchanged for a number Serbs, those who were taken prisoner in Croatia and those who were in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how this exchange was agreed upon. What I know personally was that I was subjected to interrogation - just let me finish - and that at the military investigative prison, I was awaiting to see whether charges would be lifted against me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is clear, but can you say, when you were exchanged, how many people who had been detained in Serbia were exchanged for people who had been in prisons in Croatia? Can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you precisely. I know there were 45 of us, that these were medical personnel and priests. And on the other side there was some spies from Belgrade. But as for details, you have to ask other people that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's something else I would like to ask you. Yesterday you spoke about what you had heard that people experienced, and you heard the signals they gave when what was happening was happening to them. What I want to know is, of the people you were imprisoned with in Serbia, did any of them lose their life?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not among the people who were exchanged, but I do know of people who lost their lives in camp. These, of course, were not exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the first and last name of someone who was in prison in Serbia and who lost their life?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to think about this. I can't remember exactly, but in the Stajicevo camp there was a man who was alive, and there he succumbed to the beatings, and I think that Dr. Djuranec was in that camp. I didn't see this personally, but I know it happened, although I don't remember the man's name now. Of the people who were exchanged with me, they had also been beaten and humiliated, but as to the details, you have to ask each of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were all handed over alive to the Croatian authorities, those who were with you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken by plane, and there was a gentleman, I think his name was Aco Vasiljevic, who escorted the two planes from which we arrived from Belgrade to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was my first point. My second point concerns Mrksic. Yesterday, you explained something that was connected to him. Was there any misunderstanding between you and him at the time you were negotiating the way the evacuation was to be conducted?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, there were misunderstandings, because I expected him to have the same evacuation route in front of him that I had, Vukovar, Lusac, Marinci, Bogdanovci, Nustar, Vinkovci, where buses were waiting and ambulances, but he said this was impossible, that we had go either by way of Mitrovica or Adasevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say on that occasion --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the way I was proposing couldn't be suggested because it was mined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was mined?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard from him that this was a military base towards Nustar, but I was proposing the plan agreed on with the International Red Cross. And on that Tuesday in the afternoon, he promised me that this would happen, and on the next day, Wednesday, the evacuation would take place and that that would be the route taken. That was my last conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any case, an agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was but it was not complied with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to put a question to you with respect to Sljivancanin. When you saw him for the first time, is it correct that he and another foreign humanitarian person brought in a quantity of medicines?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a Nikolas, who was a representative of the International Red Cross, a doctor, and an interpreter arrived, and they brought a truckload of aid, but in fact it was already too late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were shown a map of Vukovar, and to a question put by the Prosecutor, Mr. Nice, you responded by saying that the area under siege was 10 by 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately. I didn't measure it myself. But I can show it again on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have the map here. Within that area, was there a JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The barracks was also part of the occupation, from Borovo Selo as far as Mitnica, the present-day cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's 10 kilometres long and 3 kilometres wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the area surrounded by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the JNA used the barracks as the first point of occupation. Anything beyond the barracks, that was us. But where the barracks were, all the people had ended up in camps by then. As they took a street, they put the people in camps. We arrived when Vukovar had fallen. Some people had been in camps for two months already, who had been arrested in September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, I don't understand your answer. Let me ask you directly: Were any barracks on the territory of Vukovar surrounded by units of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any casualties among the soldiers in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as I know, not, there weren't. I was never in the barracks until I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did everything start precisely because the JNA barracks were surrounded?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I wish to put a few more questions to you in connection with the statement or, rather, your testimony in the previous case. You said awhile ago that in your hospital there was a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in the transcript from your previous testimony, that's page 425, line 3, you said the following: "During the aggression on Vukovar, during those three months of blockade, there was a crisis defence staff in the basement of the municipal building. Marin Vidic was the president. There were also others who were in charge of certain things." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you took part in the functioning of the Crisis Staff of the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on occasion, when I was invited to come and talk about supplies for the hospital. But I wasn't there all the time. The Crisis Staff had frequent sessions, probably, but I was only invited there twice. There was another doctor, Dr. Mato Sivic, who was a permanent member of the Crisis Staff. It wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in military terms?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the military commander was Mile Dedakovic in the beginning, and later on, Branko Borkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marin Vidic was a civilian commissioner of the government and Dokmanovic did not show up at work any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. On page 400, line 14 -- just a minute -- you said the following: "The area around the hospital was in fact under the control of the Croatian police and the defence of the town, but in the course of that Sunday or week..." Are you referring to the last Sunday of the siege?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, you're just giving me a sentence. What kind of statement was this? Is this testimony before this Tribunal or a statement I made in prison?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your testimony. You say: "The area around the hospital actually was under the control of the Croatian police and the defence of the city, but throughout that week, we had noticed that the number of troops was declining. They were going to the front so that, in effect, the centre of the town was left without any military defences."

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the last week before the occupation when simply there was no longer any --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say -- can you say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- how many Croatian soldiers there were in the town?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say because I never knew this. I can only tell you where the main points were from where they brought in the wounded, and that's where I communicated with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you noticed something.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We noticed that there were fewer and fewer of them. They went to try to break through, but I don't know who was where or who went Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. where. You have to ask others that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said they went to the front line. Can you tell us where front line was?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The front line was the occupation line from Mitnica, vinarija -- the winery, the barracks, then the wooden market and the hunting lodge. As far as Lusac I can tell you. Well, I know where the front line was, that's where they brought the wounded from. But how many soldiers there were and how many left, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that the entire area of 10 kilometres by 3 was the front line?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Protecting the town.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more thing: On page 408, line 9, you said in the Dokmanovic case: "They exerted pressure on me to tell them where the Croatian soldiers were. I simply didn't know who had gone, how or where." That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your statement that you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal, that is to the OTP, you spoke of the breakthrough carried out on the 17th of November. What did you mean by the word "breakthrough"?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the 17th, but this means that two weeks before Vukovar fell, people left Vukovar, and they called this "breakthrough." "Breakthrough" meant breaking out of the encirclement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said: "But the civilians were afraid to go back to their shelter because the Croatian soldiers and defenders were no longer at the front line --" or, rather, the defence line. And then you said that this was the breakthrough operation in which your son Damir also managed to get out of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can only answer the following question, please: Did you receive instructions from the Croatian government not to give any sort of information about whether there were military units or weapons there, or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never received any instructions of any kind from the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, along with all the statements that the Office of the Prosecutor has and the statement made to the investigators, there is also a statement made on the 7th of March, 1993, to a high-ranking officer from Canada, Jim Carter, who was working in the investigation team on behalf of the UN experts' team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that you told him, in that statement of 1993, that you had to keep secret or, rather, that you were not allowed to say that there were any Croatian army or soldiers or any defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have to tender this part of the statement. It's a statement made in English and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that statement at all. Who is Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To whom did I make the statement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave it to the Canadian officer who was an investigator on behalf of a team of experts of the UN.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 7th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have a look at this? I don't believe any of this. God knows what sort of paper this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got a great deal of paper in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that all these papers should have been shown to me before. I think this makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a brief statement.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what does it matter when I've never seen it before?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a sufficient number of copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. One by one. Now, what is this statement, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a statement made to investigators of the United Nations, to a high-ranking Canadian officer, in 1993. And this was recorded. There are also recordings of this. And this was disclosed to us under Article 66 -- Rule 66 by the OTP. And I wish to show only a short insert in which Dr. Bosanac said something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Show the witness just that part, just the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on page 58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're going to be shown a statement. I hope it's in a language you can understand. And you're just going to be asked a question about it. Just have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is parallel text in English and BHS -- B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is about. There is something about the construction of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This has been crossed out. Would you look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th of March, 1993. I can't identify this easily. This is some sort of transcript I did when the commission headed by Mr. Mazowiecki arrived, I did make some statements, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made this.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what specifically are you interested in here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bottom of page 58. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here, "Doctor --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. What are you talking about? In the middle, in the middle.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Major Sljivancanin told me --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "-- I want to talk to you. And I was waiting to see what he wanted to talk to me about. He asked me, Where are the members of the Croatian army? I said I don't know. How come you don't know? I don't know because -- I said I didn't know because I had received instructions from --" What?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "From the minister that there must be no Croatian soldiers." "I received instructions from the minister that there must be no Croatian soldiers."

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This has been pulled out of context. I received instructions from the minister about the evacuation, and the International Red Cross said there must be no soldiers either of the Croatian army or the JNA in the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there must be no Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hospital there must be either no Croatian soldiers and then there will be no Yugoslav soldiers. This is the context in which this was said, but I don't know what this is about. I think that this sort of questioning with this kind of foisting of evidence during the questioning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, you need have no fear. There will be no twisting of evidence here, but counsel is entitled to ask you about what he regards as differences. Now, have you finished, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think before I re-examine, it might be prudent to check on the state of exhibits, because they've been coming in at a fair number and I'm going to refer to one of them or possibly two in re-examination, and you'll need the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The registrar will need some time to get them into order, which seems reasonable. We'll do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I want to do a short exercise at a fairly early stage derived in part from an exhibit we've already looked at, which is the witness's book, our Exhibit 380. There are two things I want to ask the witness about that. If she could have the bound volume of it. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, this is a bound volume. Is this a private publication or is this a book that's on public sale, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a book, a copy of my appeals, which is to be found in the historical museum, and it was published by a publishing house, The Association of Invalids, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not to be found in book stores, but it was promoted at promotion ceremonies, and of course, the sale of the book is free.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The most grave allegations have been raised by this accused against you. You're still working at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we will discover, with some of the doctors and medical staff referred to by the accused as people who have allegedly provided evidence against you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have publicly stated your position since what happened in Vukovar included in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, it may be helpful if we look just at a short passage of the preface of the book. And if the witness could have the preface open in Croatian, and if a copy with the English preface could go on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So against the range of allegations about the Croats generally and you in particular, you published in the way described material that if we pick up the preface from about six lines down, you set out how it was a "Town of craftsmen and merchants and home for 300 families." Set out the majority of the population were Croats, Germans and Hungarians. Next sentence, "It would always be on the border of various nations." Next sentence, "Its location and tradition were the cause of multi-ethnicity." Next sentence: "However, they would never change the history and culture of this city. In 1991, during the severe aggression against the town and the people of the surrounding villages, 15.000 people remained in the town in a complete blockade." And then- and I won't take the Court's time - you set out the whole history as you understand it to be, and towards the bottom of the page, you set out what happened to the hospital and how, during the aggression, people in the hospital were treated. So you have publicly and regularly set out your position. Is that correct, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made one observation in relation to one of the challenged documents that you didn't write in capital letters. I must ask you about that and possibly correct you. First of all, there was a supplement to your statement produced by the accused that was in capital letters, and before we part from this book, at page -- sorry, I've now lost it -- it's 20 -- I'll find it. There are some capital letter entries in this book. It's ERN number 2492. Thank you very much. At the top right-hand corner. If you can find that. It's not very far in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher would be good enough to find 2492.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will find at least one of your letters is in capital letters.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that my handwriting was not the handwriting of the letter concerned. So I never write in that particular way, and that's not my handwriting. This, on the other hand, is my handwriting, yes. But the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- letter that was shown to me by Mr. Milosevic, that is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. If this is your handwriting, I'll presume to mark a copy, and I'll hand this copy, highlighted a copy. If you'd just look at it very briefly for three characters, and then we'll look at a copy of the challenged document. If we look at this, please -- could you place that on the overhead projector. Could you please it on the overhead projector, please, so that we can all see. I've highlighted on this document the K's, the J's, and the Z's, noting in particular that the Z's are not crossed. These are the K's and J's, and Z's that you write, are they, Doctor, when you write in capital letters?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you now look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I presume to have the document that was marked for identification photocopied so the original is unaffected, but for convenience it's been photocopied and I have highlighted again the same characters on this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at this one and zoom in a little bit, we'll see, for example, the J's, which are formed with two strokes, the Z's, which are all crossed, and on this document the K's, which are formed in possibly two ways but as we can see on the screen, one of those K's is formed by a down stroke and then a single curved stroke to the right of it. Are these letters, the J's, the Z's, and the K's, the way you write in capital letters or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't write this. I never write in this way. This was written by some clerk, technician. It's a different style of writing altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this letter, why it was written, making the propositions it does about, I think, the use of ambulances for military? Do you know anything about this at all?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I say, I see this for the first time here and now. Let me read through it to see why it was written. But quite certainly, I did not write this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. Despite the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. very lofty ideas Mr. Nice has about his professional capabilities, I don't consider that he is a professional and therefore able to assess the authenticity of this document. There are professionals and experts in that field, and he's not one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We note that objection. No doubt you can get some -- an expert to look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can do that. The same -- and I've only dealt with three characters in the alphabet. The same comparison can also be done with the document that has yet to be marked, which was the supplement to the witness's statement which she acknowledged was hers and that was produced in prison, which is also in capital writing. But again, the distinction between these characters and those can be found. And let me make it quite clear, now that we've looked at the document, I have no objection to the exhibit which has been marked for identification being produced as an exhibit, it being the Prosecution's case, of course through the witness, that a forgery has been produced. And I turn to other matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before the transcript disappears. Doctor, you said that this may have been written by some clerk or technician. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. I meant somebody who actually is trying to practice writing in this way. It's the kind of writing that skilled workers usually use. So it's -- I don't know how to explain it to you. Not the type of writing that anyone in the medical profession would use. Sort of semi-skilled, skilled person.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that somebody, for example, an engineer would write in this way, or an architect. They tend to write in this kind of way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your secretary or assistant, did they not write the letter in the name of yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My secretary used a typewriter, but I would always write -- sign it myself, sign the documents myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you're saying that the difference between the two handwritings is evident, it's plain to see, even without the benefit of expert --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And -- and -- but I don't rely on any opinion of my own, contrary to what the accused is suggesting. I'm relying on the evidence of the witness to whose attention I have drawn three particular characters from the alphabet and on which she has expressed her own opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have myself participated in cases where that kind of exercise is done without expert evidence, where the difference is plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm happy to see what I'm doing today accords with Your Honour's experience. But we can't take any more time on it than that. I move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement that's been shown to you, first of 112 pages and then with some supplementary additions, you haven't seen it until today. Did you ever make any attempts to get a copy of it or to see it before?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, later on, when I talked to these people from the international commission for detainees, I said that I had given a statement to that effect, and I endeavoured to obtain complete medical documents via the Foreign Ministry and the Commission for Detainees and Missing Persons. I received a very courteous letter saying that they would do their best but that the opposite side said there was no information of that kind. And as has been shown here, Mr. Milosevic did bring in some information and facts and figures from medical documents, so I should kindly like to ask the Trial Chamber to see that the complete medical documents are available as evidence, because then they'll receive the right presentation and picture of the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm just looking at the clock. Are you going to be very much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have several more questions. I won't be much longer but I have several more questions and I ought to ask them, given the gravity of the allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we understand the witness has a flight to catch, so we ought to get on as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll be as brief as I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, these grave allegations against you and those with whom you were working are made in the context of the letters that you wrote, which are revealed in your book, seeking attention from the international community who you wanted to help, and if necessary, to come to your hospital. Is there any suggestion -- is there any truth in the suggestion that you were acting in the way described, allowing people to be killed and so on, when at the same time you were bringing or doing everything you could to bring the international community to your assistance?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the allegations made here by Mr. Milosevic are true. I did everything I could to help all people, and I prevailed upon the international community to come and help us. And Vukovar was destroyed. It was full of injured persons, poor people, sick people of all ethnic groups. And had the international community arrived just one month before, many lives would have been preserved, saved. But unfortunately, it did not come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, on video, we saw Sljivancanin refusing access to the hospital to Cyrus Vance. Now, you gave an estimate of the date of that encounter, but we will have other evidence that will give the date absolutely accurately. Can you think of any valid reason, given the allegations being made against you, can you think of any valid reason for the JNA to be refusing Cyrus Vance the opportunity to inspect your hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot think of any valid reason. I can't understand. Quite obviously, the reason was to cover up the crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement with its supplements that have been produced to you, we'll have it in translation soon, I hope, and you may, if you want, have an opportunity to read it after you leave here again and make any comments to us at that stage, maybe. But tell us, was it taken by way of interrogation or was it a free statement that you wrote yourself? Just in a sentence, explain how it came to be written so the Judges can understand.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement was taken through an interrogation. Every day, all day, I was interrogated, questioned, every day and all day. I was asked questions, I was given precise instructions as to how I was to write the statement. But let me say that I wanted to write the actual state of affairs in the statement, about the shelling, about the way in which people were being killed during the occupation, however, Colonel Branko insisted upon me writing it but writing it according to his instructions. And he said the sooner I wrote the statement, the sooner I would be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, to your knowledge, include in the statement, because of the instructions of the officer, anything that you knew to be untrue at the time or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I knew at the time is what I wrote at the time. I cannot remember everything now. I would have to read through the statement again to remind myself of all the things in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It's obvious, from what you've given, that you had no knowledge at the time of making the statement of Ovcara and what had happened there. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the doctors referred to as saying things adverse to you, Dr. Zvenkovic, has he, until recently, worked at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's working there now too, but he's on sick leave. He's ill at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you get on well with him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do get on, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has he given you an explanation as to how his statement came to be prepared?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to my office himself and said that what the papers in Serbia were writing was not correct, that he never made the statements to the journalists. And then I didn't pursue it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Emejdi.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Emejdi is working there now too. I said that he was in detention in Nis, together with his father, and that he was exchanged the name day I was. I never discussed the matter with him. And he works at the hospital today too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Djuranec?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
